title: IV fluid prescribing after surgery

guidelineVersions: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital (published 2013; updated 5 May 2017)

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee on the colorectal ward. A 70-kg adult is postoperative day 2 after laparotomy and remains nil by mouth with a nasogastric tube. The nurses ask you to review the IV prescription.
brief.task: Review the clinical observations, balance and blood results supplied by the examiner; describe your initial 24-hour fluid plan and respond to new symptoms. You are not required to select a proprietary brand of fluid.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: This is a fluid-prescribing reasoning station: specify indication, volume, losses and review plan.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Confusing maintenance with additional nasogastric replacement and continuing fluids despite new pulmonary symptoms.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Decide whether IV is still indicated and inspect fluid status before choosing a bag.

flow: Check intake, observations and physical fluid status.
Distinguish routine maintenance from ongoing NG losses and deficits.
Calculate a weight-based starting plan, then adjust to electrolytes and comorbidity.
Reassess sudden breathlessness, escalate and hand over.

grid.label: Fluid indication
grid.fail: Automatically orders a bag without asking whether IV therapy is needed.
grid.borderline: Asks about oral intake but does not decide whether IV therapy is necessary.
grid.pass: Checks inability to meet needs orally and states IV fluids should stop once enteral intake is adequate.
grid.high: Explains a time-limited prescription and reviews when nausea resolves.

grid.label: Fluid status
grid.fail: Ignores hypotension or pulmonary oedema risk.
grid.borderline: Asks for BP but omits urine output and chest signs.
grid.pass: Checks observations, perfusion, oedema, chest, urine output and recent weight.
grid.high: Integrates trend, kidney function and fluid chart before any rate decision.

grid.label: Interpret losses
grid.fail: Treats the NG losses as covered by maintenance.
grid.borderline: Identifies drain output but fails to quantify volume.
grid.pass: Separates routine needs from measured NG loss and previous deficit.
grid.high: States losses should be replaced and reassessed against changing NG output.

grid.label: Maintenance calculation
grid.fail: Uses 3 litres for every patient without weight.
grid.borderline: Calculates volume but not electrolytes or glucose.
grid.pass: For 70 kg gives initial ~1750–2100 mL/day plus ~70 mmol/day each Na/K/Cl and 50–100g glucose, adjusted for clinical state.
grid.high: Explicitly excludes additional NG losses from maintenance and adjusts potassium to actual renal function/labs.

grid.label: Replacement approach
grid.borderline: Prescribes replacement without checking electrolytes or ongoing measurement.
grid.pass: Plans replacement of measured NG loss using electrolyte-appropriate fluid and repeat measurement.
grid.high: Avoids a fixed rate as losses change and obtains senior/pharmacy input for composition.

grid.label: Potassium safety
grid.fail: Adds potassium to a bag at the bedside without first checking renal function.
grid.borderline: Notices potassium but fails to cross-check latest result.
grid.pass: Reviews K 3.4 and renal function before any potassium-containing prescription; never adds K to a bag manually.
grid.high: Plans frequent checks if ongoing vomiting/NG losses cause evolving depletion.

grid.label: Prescription completeness
grid.borderline: Names a product but omits 24-hour plan.
grid.pass: Specifies fluid type, volume, rate and 24-hour review in a written plan.
grid.high: Documents reason for each component including maintenance versus replacement.

grid.label: Response to cue
grid.fail: Gives an unassessed large bolus despite new breathlessness.
grid.borderline: Stops fluid but does not examine or escalate.
grid.pass: At breathlessness cue, rechecks ABCDE and lungs, pauses/reassesses fluids and seeks senior review.
grid.high: Differentiates overload from deterioration, organises appropriate observation and urgent senior assessment.

grid.label: Monitoring and handover
grid.fail: Does not review U&Es or balance.
grid.borderline: Requests bloods without specifying timing or review.
grid.pass: Orders daily U&Es and fluid balance, checks output, reviews the plan and hands over.
grid.high: Sets clear triggers to reassess earlier if output rises or perfusion worsens.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I can prescribe a standard drip.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: I have not been able to eat.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Most people can have three litres a day, so I will order that.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The patient weighs 70 kg. NG loss is 800 mL in 24 hours, potassium 3.4. What about those losses?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The drip will cover everything; I do not need to measure what comes out.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will not replace the 800 mL of NG aspirate; it does not need its own prescription.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will ask the nurse to add potassium to the bag at the bedside; I do not need to check the renal function first.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will leave the infusion running and review this during tomorrow’s round.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will write “IV fluids” and let the nurses choose the rate.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I have no particular blood-test plan.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I have been asked to review your IV fluids. Is it alright if I ask some questions and examine you?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. I feel dry and nauseated.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you been able to drink or eat since the operation?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No, I still feel sick and have a tube draining my stomach.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Are you dizzy on sitting up, unusually breathless, or swollen in your legs?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I feel thirsty but not breathless.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will check your pulse, BP, lungs, mouth, peripheral perfusion and oedema and review the fluid balance.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Pulse 94, BP 112/70, saturations 98% air, clear lungs, no oedema. Urine 45 mL/hour. Weight 70 kg.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How much has the nasogastric tube drained, and what has the oral intake been?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: 800 mL gastric aspirate in 24 hours; no oral intake; 400 mL of IV fluid given so far today. Recent sodium 138, potassium 3.4, creatinine 76 micromol/L.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will distinguish routine maintenance from replacement of the 800 mL measured gastric loss rather than bundle them together.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For a 70-kg adult who is not frail, maintenance is 25–30 mL/kg/day, so I will plan 2,000 mL for this 24-hour period with about 70 mmol each of sodium, potassium and chloride and 50–100 g glucose. The patient has already had 400 mL today, so the remaining maintenance is 1,600 mL, not a fresh 2 litres on top.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The 800 mL measured NG loss is replaced separately, volume for volume, with 0.9% sodium chloride containing 20 mmol/L potassium chloride, because gastric fluid is chloride-rich and contains potassium. At yesterday’s rate that is about 35 mL/hour (roughly 600 mL over the remaining 18 hours), adjusted 6-hourly to the measured aspirate.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Potassium is 3.4 with normal creatinine (76) and urine output of 45 mL/hour, so potassium-containing fluid is appropriate. I will use pre-mixed potassium bags only; I would never put loose potassium into an IV bag.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Prescription for the remaining 18 hours: line 1, maintenance, 1,600 mL 0.18% sodium chloride/4% glucose with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at 90 mL/hour (about 64 mmol potassium, 48 mmol sodium, 64 g glucose); line 2, NG replacement, 0.9% sodium chloride with 20 mmol/L potassium chloride matched to measured losses, starting at 35 mL/hour. That is about 76 mmol potassium in total, appropriate with K 3.4 and ongoing losses. I will document each line’s purpose and review time, and ask the senior surgeon or pharmacist if a specialist formulation is needed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: At minute seven the patient says: “I have just started feeling short of breath.”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will stop and reassess: ABCDE, saturations, BP, lungs, fluid balance and urine output, pause further non-urgent fluids while reviewing, and escalate urgently if there is respiratory compromise.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will monitor observations, strict input and output including each new NG aspirate volume, daily weight where useful, and at least daily U&Es, sooner if losses or physiology change.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Will I need the drip forever?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No. We will switch back to drinking when it is safe and you can meet your needs.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please summarise your prescription safety-net.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Maintenance, measured replacement, fluid status and electrolytes are four separate checks; review after the next blood results and sooner for breathlessness, oliguria or increased NG output.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I want to prescribe only the fluids you need, and reassess daily. May I check a few things?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Yes. I am thirsty and the NG tube keeps collecting fluid.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: What have you managed orally since yesterday?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Nothing.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any dizziness, worsening abdominal pain, swollen ankles or breathing problems?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Just thirst and nausea; I can breathe fine.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will first review the vital-sign trend and examine perfusion, mucosae, lungs and oedema, as fluid charts alone can mislead.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: BP 112/70, pulse 94, clear chest, no oedema; urine 45 mL/hour. Weight 70 kg.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How much measured loss, and what was administered?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: NG aspirate 800 mL in the last 24 hours, no oral intake, 400 mL IV so far; Na 138, K 3.4, creatinine 76.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can separate three issues: maintenance while nil by mouth, replacement of continuing gastric losses, and a search for evidence of an existing deficit. I do not have evidence that this stable patient needs an immediate resuscitation bolus.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Initial maintenance: 25–30 mL/kg/day means 1750–2100 mL per day at 70 kg; approximate electrolyte needs are 1 mmol/kg/day for each of sodium, potassium and chloride, plus 50–100 g glucose. These are starting targets, not a one-size-fits-all formula.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The NG tube is an additional, changing loss. I would measure it each shift, choose fluid/electrolyte replacement in line with results and unit policy, and review it with the senior team instead of using the same bag indefinitely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The potassium of 3.4 makes loss replacement important, but I must reassess renal function and potassium before prescribing any potassium-containing fluid. I will never add potassium to a bag at the bedside.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will write the prescription with bag composition, total volume and rate, plus a 24-hour plan spelling out what is maintenance and what replaces measured losses; I will document the review time.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Can the drip be stopped when I can drink again?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Yes. IV fluid is temporary; we will reduce and stop it once oral or enteral intake can safely meet your needs.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The patient suddenly says: “I have just become short of breath.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is new. I would pause non-essential infusion, reassess ABCDE, oxygenation, chest signs and input/output, and urgently involve the senior team if respiratory compromise or overload is suspected; I would not assume the original plan is still correct.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will follow urine output, balance, daily weight if meaningful, repeat sodium, potassium and creatinine at least daily, and earlier for rapidly changing NG losses or new deterioration.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Give a final one-line handover.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Stable, nil by mouth, 800 mL NG loss and K 3.4: calculated maintenance plus separately measured replacement, defined monitoring and immediate reassessment if breathless or oliguric.

failures.move: Treats 800 mL gastric loss as if it did not exist.
failures.consequence: Progressive dehydration, electrolyte depletion or inadequate replacement.

failures.move: Continues an unassessed infusion when the patient newly develops breathlessness.
failures.consequence: Possible worsening fluid overload or missed acute deterioration.

failures.move: Writes no specific rate, volume or review time.

recovery.when: If you mixed maintenance and replacement
recovery.line: I have mixed maintenance and replacement; I will stop and prescribe them as separately measurable components.

recovery.when: If the patient has become breathless
recovery.line: The patient has become breathless, so I am reassessing the fluid prescription and respiratory status before continuing.

knowledge.fact: IV fluids are indicated only when oral/enteral routes cannot meet needs.
The 5 Rs include resuscitation, routine maintenance, replacement, redistribution and reassessment.

Standard initial maintenance is 25–30 mL/kg/day, approximately 1 mmol/kg/day each Na/K/Cl and 50–100 g/day glucose; consider less (e.g. 20–25 mL/kg/day) if older or frail, or with renal or cardiac impairment.
Ongoing abnormal losses need separate replacement and repeated review.
A fluid prescription needs product, volume and rate plus a 24-hour management and monitoring plan.
Fluid monitoring includes fluid status, fluid balance and laboratory assessment.

recall.think: Why IV today, and what is additional to maintenance?
recall.say: “I will separate routine fluid needs from measured losses.”
do: Examine, calculate, prescribe precisely, and reassess after the next results.
recall.trap: The same bag cannot cover an unmeasured, changing NG loss indefinitely.
recall.finish: Document review triggers and aim to stop IV fluids when oral intake is adequate.

sources.name: NICE CG174, Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital

partner.opening: Please review this postoperative IV fluid chart.
partner.actorBrief: The patient initially reports thirst and nausea, but no breathlessness.

reveals.trigger: When asked (do not volunteer numerical losses before candidate requests fluid chart or examiner observations)
reveals.finding: no oral intake; 800 mL NG output during 24 hours; total IV so far today 400 mL; urine 45 mL/hour; 70 kg; pulse 94, BP 112/70, saturation 98% room air; chest clear; no oedema. Na 138, K 3.4, creatinine 76 micromol/L.

reveals.trigger: Assumptions for the worked prescription (give if asked)
reveals.finding: the fluid chart runs 08:00–08:00 and it is now 14:00, so 18 hours remain; the 400 mL already given was Hartmann’s; the patient is not frail and has no cardiac or renal impairment; examination shows no deficit needing correction.

reveals.trigger: If asked for new observations before response
reveals.finding: saturations 95% room air and respiratory rate 24; no unprompted diagnosis.

curveballs.prompt: At around minute seven ONLY: patient says, “I have just started feeling short of breath.”
curveballs.safeAnswer: At breathlessness cue, rechecks ABCDE and lungs, pauses/reassesses fluids and seeks senior review.
